note_tweet.text:
Now that the jam is over, I have more time to focus on the problems that slowed my workflow and held me back. So I started building GameLens.

GameLens joins Claude and Unreal Engine 5.9. Built in one night with Claude Code, three versions, tested on STILL, my jam game.

What held me back:
• Every agent session rediscovered STILL call by call. Unreal 5.9's MCP toolset list alone is 34,330 characters before any work starts.
• My scripted tests passed all day while no key worked for me. One test passed 55 checks with the boy out of the picture.
• About 200 of the 964 scripts in my Tools folder were workarounds.

What it does:
• Reads the whole project as text: STILL's 586 assets and 13 maps in about 15 s, also while the editor is closed. It reads the Animation, Widget and level-script Blueprints that 5.9's own Blueprint tool refuses.
• Plays the game through real input, like a keyboard, and writes down what changed: camera, widgets, sounds, errors, map travel.
• Looks at the picture: numbered boxes, plus rays from the camera that say what fills the frame and flag the edge of the set, near objects and objects resting on nothing.
• Files a bug ticket on F9: the picture, a labelled copy, game state, the last 60 seconds from a black box, errors, my recent editor actions, the build.
• Runs render A/Bs (DLSS, DLAA, TSR) with GPU times and a stillness score.

What it found:
• 32x less to read. On 7 real questions about STILL, the native MCP read 180,563 characters. GameLens read 5,718.
• The native Blueprint tool refused the boy's Animation Blueprint and BP_StillBoy itself. One question cost it 22 calls and 161,330 characters. GameLens: 1 call, 875.
• Reading a Blueprint through the native graph text marks it unsaved. A one-value edit through it dropped a node: 107 before, 106 after.
• On Reel 1's opening, inspect flagged the edge of the set: nothing behind 3.6% of the picture at the top, and dark there.
• In a freshly started editor, the first 3 s of play came from the world origin at floor level, with grey stand-in materials. The bug key caught it on its first real use.
• DLSS on my RTX 4060 Ti, Reel 1's opening, paused, GPU time, mean of 3 runs: TSR 6.2 ms, DLAA 5.8, DLSS Quality 4.9, DLSS Performance 4.5. That saves 1.3 to 1.6 ms and no frames: the editor's game thread holds this shot at about 90 to 115 fps. In the paused scene, DLSS Performance never held still.
• Its first DLSS test took five fixes to get right: the editor's override, film grain and motion, thumbnails, an animated menu, textures still streaming. Its floating-object check was wrong too.

What it does not catch yet: a white plastic chair stands against the fence in the opening shot, facing the planks. Every check asked "is it there, does it render", none asked "does it make sense". Scene-logic rules are next.

STILL, free on Windows: https://t.co/umNHIA3S8x

My daughter’s school promised a pizza party to every kid who sold 20 boxes of cookie dough.

Thirty one kids in her grade. Nine hit the goal. Lily sold 3.

We live on the third floor of an apartment building, and I work nights at a warehouse where nobody has a kid at her school. The night before the deadline, I had my cursor on the button to buy the other 17 boxes myself. $204. I closed the tab.

On Friday, the nine kids ate pizza in the gym. The other twenty-two sat in the library with a worksheet and a bag of pretzels.

Lily told me about it in the car, in a voice so flat I almost missed it.

“Dad, the pizza smell came under the door.”

Then she said, “But something happened.”

FaenoCAD has a way out of drawings for ME design. 

Imagine, for a moment, a world where you have a single source of truth file, which holds all the information necessary to build a part. The basic standard has been around forever. STEP AP242 is perfect for this. 

The role of drawings in ME design has been critically viewed for at least the last 20 years. PTC, back in the 2000s or before, anticipated MBD, had all GD&T annotations available in the model window. 

Everyone used drawings anyway. 

We finally have ERP systems which can hold everything together, and computers are ubiquitous, so we can all view and rotate a model without resorting to workstations. 

Drawings are still common for those outside bespoke organizations. 

How to close the gap? 

Use STEP as the single source of truth. All MBD information is there. Add annotations and notes to the file all you want. Agentic AI uncovers it for users, makes it human readable without special software. 

STEP can be grepped just like any other text file. Claude writes a report. Claude can build you a fully dimensioned drawing from this, if you want. But more interestingly, it can build you just the views which show annotations and tolerances of interest. 

I post about drawings and their role in ME design because there are people out there making products which just barf dimensions on a page and call it a day. Some are even advertising their shitty-ass drawings as demos. These people are not skating to where the puck is going. They are assuming people just want to create drawings faster. 

You don't use AI to speed up your "create drawings" workflow. You use AI to enable MBD without specialized ERP or software. Point Claude Code to a STEP MBD and let it uncover all the tolerancing and annotation information in whatever format you please. 

Keep the single source of truth file. Make MBD ubiquitous, even for the little players.

Your coding agent fixes the bug. A teammate opens a fresh environment and cannot reproduce the result. Was the task actually finished?

Mitchell Hashimoto’s Rex post raises a useful point: remote development and production are connected problems, not just two places to run a terminal.

For an AI coding handoff, I’d want four things beside the patch:
• the exact commit and dependency lockfile
• setup steps without embedded secrets
• the test command and its result
• what survives when the remote session disappears

“Works on my agent” should not become the new “works on my machine.”

Source: https://t.co/7ZYme6j3br

A thousand years ago, I made a dent in dev envs with “Vagrant.” The most popular request always was “I want Vagrant for remote envs.” I’ve been asked this to this day!! I tried and failed many times. I made things that worked but didn’t work right. Well, Rex is done right. Rex is my answer, finally. 

It’s always lived in the back of my mind no matter what I did. I would come up with something and try it and it didn’t feel right. 

I got really close around 5 years ago to the point I setup a website branding etc (via HashiCorp). But at the last minute I pulled it. It still wasn’t right. I couldn’t explain why and didn’t have a better solution. I just knew it had to be binned. 

Well, Rex is it. This is the real deal. 

Rex is doing for remote development (and a lot more than just dev) what I think a proper solution should’ve done. It’s far more than just a dev tool but I think part of what I knew is once you reach into remote environments that line isn’t clear anymore. You have to solve both remote dev and remote prod. 

Here we go, back to the beginning.
